/*
# The site's faces

The type the homepage and the pages it hosts are set in, named once. A face is a
**stack** — the families in order of preference, exactly as `fontFamily` itself
takes them — so it is a theme token like any other, and a program reads one
with `Faces.helvetica`.

```declare-fragment
App [ fontFamily = { Faces.helvetica }, … ]
```

A list is a token because a token is bounded, plain data, and an ordered list of
family names is that. Writing the stack as one comma-joined string would work
too, but then the fallback order is a convention inside a string rather than
something the checker can see.

Two faces, because the homepage offers a type tuner: Helvetica is the site's,
Avenir the alternative under assessment.
*/

theme Faces [
    // The conventional Helvetica stack: the real face on Apple devices, Arial on
    // Windows; on Linux, fontconfig maps both names to its metric-compatible
    // lookalikes, and anything else falls to the system sans.

    helvetica = ["Helvetica Neue", "Helvetica", "Arial", "sans-serif"],

    // Avenir Next ships only on Apple platforms; elsewhere this falls to the
    // system face.

    avenir = ["Avenir Next", "Avenir", "system-ui", "sans-serif"]
    ]

/*
# SimpleLayout — stack children along an axis

The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and this stack obeys it without
knowing it exists: it arranges inside the room the view gives it, so a run
placed at `0` starts at the content origin, the cross-axis band `align` works
in is the room *between* the insets, and a view that sizes itself from the
stack grows by both. The inset reaches **every** child, on both axes,
`align = none` included — a child placing its own `x = 0` sits on the content
edge, not the view's, because the content box is the parent's and not this
arrangement's.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

## axis
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

## spacing
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

## align
The **cross axis** — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none` (the default) leaves it to the
children, who place themselves with the ordinary `y = center`. `start | center | end`
aligns every child within the **band**: the view's own cross **content** extent — so a
column `width = 260` centres a `width = { parent.width - 32 }` child at 16, with the slack
split evenly — falling back to the **line**, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view
that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this
arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line *is* that extent). A
child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides.
`baseline` — a row only — sits every child on one
baseline: a `Text` reports its own, and a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`); a laid child that declares none is
refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A bare
literal.

## place()
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless `align` says
otherwise** — then the boxes carry that slot too, and own it. Override it in a subclass
for custom geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the
one place that is allowed.
*/

class SimpleLayout extends Layout [
    axis: Axis = y,
    spacing: number = 0,
    align: CrossAlign = none,

    place() {
        const axis = this.axis
        const size = axis == "x" ? "width" : "height"
        const kids = this.laid()
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true

        // slack, only when someone flexes: the view's extent along the axis
        // minus the rigid content and the gaps between visible children.
        // A child's slot is its footprint (the scale/rotation-composed box),
        // so a scale = 0.5 child occupies half the run and a rotated card
        // reserves what it visibly covers; the box's lead compensates the
        // transform's own offset so the visible edge lands on the slot
        let each = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && flexing(c)) flexN = flexN + 1
        if (flexN > 0) {
            let content = 0
            let visN = 0
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                visN = visN + 1
                if (!flexing(c)) content = content + (c).footprint()[size]
            }
            const extent = this.contentExtent(size)
            each = Math.max(0, (extent - content - this.spacing * Math.max(0, visN - 1)) / flexN)
        }

        // the cross axis, when `align` claims it: children align within the
        // BAND — the view's own cross extent, or the largest laid cross extent
        // when the view measures these very children (viewExtent answers 0 on
        // that view: reading an extent this pass feeds is the cycle the
        // one-pass discipline forbids, and there the two agree anyway).
        // Math.max keeps an over-wide child from hanging out both sides.
        // A baseline line is the deepest declared one.
        const al = this.align
        const cross = axis == "x" ? "y" : "x"
        const crossSize = axis == "x" ? "height" : "width"
        let line = 0
        let lineBase = 0
        if (al != "none") {
            if (al == "baseline" && axis != "x") this.refuseStackBaseline()
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                line = Math.max(line, (c).footprint()[crossSize])
                const b = (c).baseline
                if (al == "baseline" && typeof b == "number") lineBase = Math.max(lineBase, b)
            }
            // `start` places at the band's origin and `baseline` on the shared
            // line — neither reads the band, so only center/end ask for it
            if (al == "center" || al == "end") line = Math.max(line, this.viewExtent(crossSize))
        }

        let pos = 0
        return kids.map((c) => {
            const flex = c.visible && flexing(c)
            // footprint, never bounds: the strategy must not read the slot it
            // writes (one-pass discipline). A flexing child's size is allocated
            // (box.w/h), so its footprint is never consulted — lead 0, raw slot.
            const f = flex ? null : (c).footprint()
            const lead = f == null ? 0 : (axis == "x" ? f.x : f.y)
            const box = (axis == "x" ? ({ x: pos - lead }) : ({ y: pos - lead }))
            if (flex) box[axis == "x" ? "w" : "h"] = each
            if (al != "none") {
                // start = the line's origin; center/end offset the child's
                // footprint within the line; baseline sits the child's declared
                // baseline on the line's — a child with none is refused, once,
                // and placed at start (the arrangement never breaks)
                const fc = f == null ? (c).footprint() : f
                const leadC = axis == "x" ? fc.y : fc.x
                let off = 0
                if (al == "center") off = (line - fc[crossSize]) / 2
                else if (al == "end") off = line - fc[crossSize]
                else if (al == "baseline" && axis == "x") {
                    const b = (c).baseline
                    if (typeof b == "number") off = lineBase - b
                    else if (c.visible) this.refuseBaseline(c)
                }
                box[cross] = off - (al == "baseline" ? 0 : leadC)
            }
            if (c.visible) pos = pos + (flex ? each : (f)[size]) + this.spacing
            return box
            })
        }
    ]

# ResponsiveLayout — arrange children differently at different widths.

A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. **`share` divides width in either flow** — in a
row it apportions the run; in a stack it sets how wide each band is, as a
plain percentage of the view. The names are the view's own child names,
checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is a loud
error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **a share of `0` drops that child
while the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is
just a number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the
view widens. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry its
own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children keep
their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**A plan need not name every child, and 20% means 20% of what is left.** A
child the plan leaves out keeps its natural width and the flow just places
it — and the run a row's shares divide is what remains **after the gaps and
after those naturals**. So a fixed-width logo beside two proportional regions
composes without the author computing a percentage for the logo:

    layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 10, plan = { [
        { from: 0, flow: "row", share: { nav: 60, actions: 40 } },
    ] } ],
    logo:    View [ width = 200 ],          // not named: keeps its 200
    nav:     Nav  [ ],                      // 60% of what is left
    actions: Actions [ ],                   // 40% of what is left

In an 880-wide bar that is 200 for the logo and 396 / 264 for the two
regions — the row fills, exactly. Change the logo's width and the regions
answer; they were never told about it.

**`share: { logo: "auto" }` says that out loud.** The word means precisely
what leaving the child out means — keep its natural size, divide the rest —
so it buys no new geometry, only legibility: the plan reads as a complete
statement of the row, and a name in a plan is checked against the tree, where
an omission is mentioned nowhere. It is **not** `share: 0`, which is the
opposite: `0` drops the child and reclaims its space, `"auto"` keeps the
child at the size it chose for itself. In a stack `"auto"` is accepted and
changes nothing — the flow axis there is height, which a share never touches.

**Two shares are refused, where the plan is read** — both of them mistakes
with no arrangement they could mean, and both silent before. A row's shares
divide one run, so a row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming
the plan and the total, rather than a row that runs its children off the end.
And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor the word `"auto"` is
an error naming the child, rather than a `NaN` width on it and a `NaN`
position on its neighbours.

**The two things authors miss.** `share` is not row-only: a `"stack"` entry
may carry shares too, and they set each band's width — the narrow plan above
could say `{ from: 0, flow: "stack", share: { logo: 100, nav: 100 } }` to make
both bands full-bleed. (A stack's shares are independent percentages of the
view, not slices of one run, which is why two hundreds are fine there and a
row's total is held to 100.) And `share: 0` is the whole of "hide it when
it's tight": a child dropped this way leaves the flow entirely and its space
is reclaimed, so there is no reason to branch a tree on a width
(`narrow ? … : …`) — appearing and disappearing is one number in one plan,
and the plan is the only place the breakpoint is written down.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it.
Shares are cut from what the naturals leave, so shares adding to 100 leave no
slack at all and a `Spacer` beside them collapses — *shares fill; naturals
align.*

**Across the flow, the layout places every child** — `y` in a row, `x` in a
stack, in every plan. Where each one sits there is the layout's `align`:
`start` unless it says otherwise, and a plan entry may say otherwise for its
own tier. A plan entry's `offset` shifts one named child from where `align`
put it — a nudge that belongs to that arrangement, so it goes away with the
tier, which is exactly when it stops meaning anything:

    actions: View [ width = 100%,
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 420, flow: "row",   gap: 18, align: "center", offset: { source: 1 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack", gap: 14 },
        ] } ],
        run:    Button [ width = 240, height = 46 ],   // the row centres the pair on it
        source: Text   [ text = "View & edit source →" ],
    ]

So a child under a ResponsiveLayout declares neither `x` nor `y` — the
checker says so at the line, and says which of these to use instead. A child
that needs a finer arrangement of its own contents is the next case down:
give it a layout of its own.

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

This is the answer to most things a plan cannot say by itself, and it wants no
class: an **ordinary inline child** carries its own `layout:` like any other
view. A component nested this way answers to **its allocation, not the
window** — the same child reads correctly in a sidebar, a dialog, or a
full-bleed row, and picks its own flow in each. One thing to get right: the
parent's plan must actually **give** the child a width in every tier. A tier
that allocates it nothing leaves it at its content width, and a child sized by
its content is measuring what it is trying to arrange — so name it in the
stack tier's shares (`share: { acts: 100 }`) or give it `width = 100%`.

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages **named regions**. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**Padding, and what `from` then means.** The inset is the view's
(`View.padding`), and a plan is selected against the **content** width, with
the shares dividing it — so a padded bar's tiers answer to the room its
children actually get, and `from: 600` means 600 of usable room, not 600 of
outer width.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Reach for **nesting** first, and most of the time last: give the part that
needs its own mind a `layout:` of its own and let it arrange itself inside the
room this plan hands it (above). A child that decides for itself is almost
always the answer to "this plan cannot say what I need", and it composes — the
same child then reads correctly wherever it is put.

Past that: whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State`
applied on a width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding
`place()` — the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

## plan
The storyboard: a list of `{ from, flow, share?, gap?, align?, offset? }` entries. **`from` means "use
this plan when the view is at least this wide"** — the largest `from` that fits wins,
wherever it sits in the list, and `from: 0` is the fallback. `flow` is `"row"` or
`"stack"`. **`share` divides width in either flow** — not row-only: a `"stack"` entry may
carry shares, and they set each band's width. It names the children by their **own child
names**, checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error.
**A share of `0` drops that child while the plan is active** — out of the flow, its space
reclaimed — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is one number rather than a
`narrow ? … : …` branch, and they return by themselves when the view widens.

**A child a plan does not name keeps its natural width, and a row's shares divide what
is left after it** — the gaps and the naturals both come out before the percentages are
cut, so `60` means 60% of the remainder and a fixed-width logo composes beside two
proportional regions with no arithmetic by hand. `"auto"` is the word for that said out
loud (`share: { logo: "auto", nav: 60, actions: 40 }`): identical geometry to leaving the
child out, and the opposite of `0` — `0` drops the child, `"auto"` keeps it at the size
it chose for itself. In a stack `"auto"` is accepted and changes nothing, since a stack's
shares are widths and its flow axis is height.

**`align` and `offset` are per tier.** A plan entry's `align` — a string, `"start"`,
`"center"`, `"end"` or `"baseline"` — overrides the layout's own for that tier, as
its `gap` does. Its `offset` names children the way `share` does and shifts each one
**across the flow** — down in a row, right in a stack — by a signed number of pixels
from where `align` placed it. A name with no child, or an offset that is not a number,
is an error naming it.

**Two values are refused where the plan is read.** A row whose shares add to more than
100 is an error naming the plan and the total — a row's shares divide one run and cannot
claim more of it than there is. (A stack's do not compete: each is an independent percent
of the view, so `{ logo: 100, nav: 100 }` is the full-bleed idiom, not an overflow — but a
single share above 100 is refused in either flow.) And a share that is neither a number
from 0 to 100 nor `"auto"` is an error naming the child, instead of a `NaN` width.

## gap
The default space between children, overridable per plan entry.

## align
Where children sit **across the flow** — `y` in a row, `x` in a stack: `start` (the
default), `center`, `end`, or `baseline`. A bare literal here; a plan entry overrides
it with a string (`align: "center"`). `center` and `end` work in the **band**: the
view's own cross content extent, or the tallest (widest) laid child on a view that sizes
itself from these very children — the same band as `SimpleLayout`'s `align`.
`baseline` sits every child of a row on one text line, each child declaring its own
(a `Text` does; a composite says which part carries it), and is refused on a stack
tier, which has no line. **There is no `none`**: this layout places the cross axis in
every tier, so it always says where.

## place()
Selects the active plan from the **view's own width — never the window's** — and
arranges accordingly: both axes of every child, along the flow by the plan and across
it by `align` and `offset`. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much
room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A
plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business.
*/

class ResponsiveLayout extends Layout [
    plan: array = { [] },
    gap: number = 10,
    align: CrossAlign = start,

    place() {
        const view = this.view
        // the room the plan divides — the view's content box, its width less
        // its own padding (contentExtent); a plan's `from` therefore reads the room,
        // which is the number its shares are cut from
        const W = this.contentExtent("width")
        const kids = this.laid()
        const plans = (Array.isArray(this.plan) ? this.plan : [])

        // The active plan: the largest `from` that fits, wherever it sits in
        // the list; nothing fits → the smallest `from` (the nearest regime).
        let tier = null
        for (const t of plans) { const f = t.from ?? 0; if (W >= f && (tier == null || f > (tier.from ?? 0))) tier = t }
        if (tier == null) for (const t of plans) { if (tier == null || (t.from ?? 0) < (tier.from ?? 0)) tier = t }
        if (tier == null) tier = ({ flow: "row" })

        const stack = tier.flow == "stack"
        const gap = typeof tier.gap == "number" ? tier.gap : this.gap
        const share = tier.share != null && typeof tier.share == "object" ? tier.share : ({})
        const where = " (the plan from " + (tier.from ?? 0) + ", on " + view.constructor.name + ")"

        // Across the flow this layout places every child, in every tier — a
        // row writes `y`, a stack `x` — so there is always an answer to where
        // a child sits there, and it is `align`: the tier's, else the layout's.
        const al = tier.align != null ? tier.align : this.align
        if (al != "start" && al != "center" && al != "end" && al != "baseline") {
            throw new Error("align is " + JSON.stringify(al) + where + " — a ResponsiveLayout places both axes of its children, so it always says where they sit across the flow: \"start\", \"center\", \"end\" or \"baseline\"")
        }

        // Resolve the share names against the view's own children — loudly —
        // and admit exactly two kinds of value: a percentage, and the word
        // "auto" ("keep this child at its natural size, divide the rest"),
        // which is carried by the plan and then means precisely what leaving
        // the child out means. Anything else is a mistake and is refused
        // here, because unrefused it would reach the arithmetic and come out
        // the other side as a NaN width on that child and a NaN x on its
        // neighbours, silently.
        const shares = new Map()
        let total = 0
        for (const name of Object.keys(share)) {
            const c = view[name]
            if (c == null || kids.indexOf(c) < 0) {
                throw new Error("the plan names '" + name + "', but " + view.constructor.name + " has no laid child named '" + name + "'")
            }
            const v = share[name]
            if (v === "auto") continue
            if (typeof v != "number" || !isFinite(v) || v < 0 || v > 100) {
                throw new Error("the share for '" + name + "' is " + JSON.stringify(v) + where + " — a share is a number from 0 to 100 (and 0 drops the child), or the word \"auto\" to keep the child at its natural size")
            }
            shares.set(c, v)
            total = total + v
        }
        // A ROW's shares divide one run, so together they cannot claim more
        // than it — the sum is checked. A STACK's do not compete: each is an
        // independent band width, a plain percent of the view, and `100, 100`
        // (both bands full-bleed) is the documented idiom. Only the row is a
        // budget, so only the row has a total.
        if (!stack && total > 100 + 1e-6) {
            throw new Error("the row's shares add up to " + (Math.round(total * 100) / 100) + "%" + where + " — the shares of a row divide one run and cannot claim more than 100% of it; a child that should keep its natural size is named \"auto\" or left out of the share")
        }

        // An offset names a child the same way a share does, and shifts it
        // across the flow from where `align` put it — a nudge that belongs to
        // this tier's arrangement, so it leaves with the tier.
        const offsets = new Map()
        const offset = tier.offset != null && typeof tier.offset == "object" ? tier.offset : ({})
        for (const name of Object.keys(offset)) {
            const c = view[name]
            if (c == null || kids.indexOf(c) < 0) {
                throw new Error("the plan's offset names '" + name + "', but " + view.constructor.name + " has no laid child named '" + name + "'")
            }
            const v = offset[name]
            if (typeof v != "number" || !isFinite(v)) {
                throw new Error("the offset for '" + name + "' is " + JSON.stringify(v) + where + " — an offset is a number of pixels across the flow, from where align places the child")
            }
            offsets.set(c, v)
        }

        const hidden = (c) => shares.get(c) === 0
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true && !hidden(c)

        // What the shares divide, in a row: the width left after the gaps
        // between the visible children AND after the children the plan does
        // not allocate — one left out of the share, or named "auto", keeps
        // its natural width, and the shares are cut from what remains. That
        // is what makes "20%" mean 20% of what is left, so a fixed-width logo
        // composes beside two proportional regions with no arithmetic by
        // hand. (In a stack the flow axis is height, which a share never
        // touches, and a share is simply a percent of the view's width — so
        // naturals never compete for it and the base is the whole width.)
        let visN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && !hidden(c)) visN = visN + 1
        const avail = W - gap * Math.max(0, visN - 1)
        let naturalRun = 0
        if (!stack) {
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible || hidden(c) || flexing(c) || shares.has(c)) continue
                naturalRun = naturalRun + (c).footprint().width
            }
        }
        const base = Math.max(0, avail - naturalRun)
        const shareW = (c) => (stack ? W : base) * (shares.get(c)) / 100

        // Rigid content along the flow axis, to size the spacers: widths in a
        // row (a share is a width), the children's own heights in a stack.
        let rigid = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) {
            if (!c.visible || hidden(c)) continue
            if (flexing(c)) { flexN = flexN + 1; continue }
            // natural sizes are the footprint (scale/rotation composed,
            // position-free); a share or flex allocation stays the raw slot it
            // claims — the strategy never reads a slot it writes
            rigid = rigid + (stack ? (c).footprint().height : (shares.has(c) ? shareW(c) : (c).footprint().width))
        }
        const room = stack ? this.contentExtent("height") - gap * Math.max(0, visN - 1) : avail
        const each = flexN > 0 ? Math.max(0, room - rigid) / flexN : 0

        // THE CROSS AXIS. Each child's extent across the flow — its footprint,
        // unless this pass allocates the child a size (a share writes its
        // width, a spacer its flow size), in which case the footprint would
        // read a slot this pass writes: then the raw cross slot, or in a stack

redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,

class Card extends View [
    // the design-token record, a provided value: the app provides it once and
    // this widget reads it. Default = the house look.

    theme: Theme = { this.$provided("theme", SanFrancisco) },

    fill = { this.theme.surface },
    cornerRadius = { this.theme.controlRadius },
    stroke = { stroke(1, this.theme.line) },

    // The inset that saves the wrapper view: the card's own content box, so
    // every child's x/y is measured from inside it — the stacked ones, and a
    // child that places itself across the card alike. The inset is the view's,
    // not the arrangement's, which is what lets a child ignore the layout and
    // still sit inside the padding.

    padding = 16,

    // The default arrangement — a plain stack, inside the room above.

    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ]

/*
# Control

The interaction-state base every stateful control extends. It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and
nothing semantic: `checked`, `value`, and their kin live on the concrete control.

The pointer half is the language's: `hovered` and `pressed` are View's read-only
interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is
the control policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads:

- `hot` / `down` — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by `disabled`, with the
  keyboard-activation `flash` folded into `down`. Style against these, not the raw
  intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up.
- `disabled` — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it.
- keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same `press()`
  path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look.

It also owns two things every labelled control shares:

- `iconLeft` / `iconRight` — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays
  them out; Control only declares that they exist, so every control that shows
  one names it the same way.
- `menu` — the **role** of dropping a menu, not decoration. Setting `menu` gets
  the disclosure mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and
  ArrowDown-to-open together, which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong
  one piece at a time.

Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated,
and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships:

```declare
class Stepper extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6,
    n: number = 0,
    fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control },
    press() { n = n + 1 },
    onClick() { if (!disabled) press() },
    t: TextLabel [ x = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ]
    ]


App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]
```

## theme
The design-token record every widget styles off — a **provided value**. An app
provides it once (`App [ theme = { app.dark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco } ]`)
and `Control` reads it here, so a control body reads `theme.accent` as a plain,
typed member. The default is `SanFrancisco`, so a control in an app that never
mentions a theme still renders. Provide a different record on a subtree to reskin
it; every `provided("theme")` below reads the nearer one.

## disabled
Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into `hot`/`down` so a
disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `theme.disabledOpacity`.

## hot
Hover under control policy — `hovered` gated by `disabled`. **Style against this, not
the raw `hovered` intrinsic**, or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always
false on touch, since `hovered` is.

## down
The pressed look — the `pressed` intrinsic gated by `disabled`, **with keyboard
activation folded in**, so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press
gives. The other half of the styling pair with `hot`.

## focused
True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the *ring*, you want nothing: the
app-level `FocusRing` indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own
focus styling.

## focusVisible
Focused **and** the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's `:focus-visible` channel.
Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no
keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a `Pane` header's focus edge reads.

## iconLeft
A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it.

## iconRight
The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as `iconLeft`. Setting it **wins over the
chevron a `menu` would imply** — see `rightIcon`.

## menu
The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (`menu = { app.optionsMenu }`).
Setting it is a *role*, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below
the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. **Declare
one menu and point many controls at it** rather than one per opener; the menu reads
`opener` to vary its items.

## menuOpen
True while `menu` is showing *and* this control is what opened it. **Derived, never
written** — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way
(Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open
look forever.

## rightIcon
What actually renders on the right: `iconRight` when set, else the disclosure chevron
implied by `menu`, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control
wears the same mark.

## flash
The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, since the `pressed` intrinsic
is the pointer's truth and is read-only. Folded into `down`, so styling needs to read
only the pair.

## flashMs
How long `flashPress()` holds the pressed look.

## openMenu()
Opens `menu` anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled.
The seam a concrete control calls from its own `press()`.

there is one. A value control delivers through `input` from here and **never writes its

constraint.

## flashPress()
Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention
for buttons and menu items. **Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback
(Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it.**

## onFocus
Records focus and captures the keyboard modality into `focusVisible`. An override must
keep both or the focus channel goes dark.

## onBlur
Clears `focused` and `focusVisible`.

## onPointerDown
Claims focus, clears the `:focus-visible` channel, and opens `menu` if there is one —
menus open on **press**, not release, as the platform does. **An override must keep the
`Focus.focus(this)` call**, or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere.

## onKeyDown
Space and Enter run `press()`; ArrowDown opens `menu`. Ignores auto-repeat.

## focusable
A control takes focus unless it is disabled — one rule, so a disabled control drops out of the Tab order without saying so twice.
*/

class Control extends View [
    // The design-token record every widget styles off — a provided value: the
    // app provides it once (`App [ theme = { … } ]`) and Control reads it here,
    // so a widget body reads `theme.accent` as a plain, typed member. The
    // default is `SanFrancisco`, so a widget in an app that never mentions a
    // theme still renders — the visible library default.

    theme: Theme = { this.$provided("theme", SanFrancisco) },

    disabled: boolean = false,
    focused:  boolean = false,

    // A control is chrome, not prose: its label never selects, even inside a
    // `selectable` region (a provision here vetoes the inherited value — the
    // language rule: anything that activates declares itself unselectable).

    selectable = false,

    // the styling pair — the interaction intrinsics under control policy

    hot:  boolean = { this.hovered && !this.disabled },
    down: boolean = { (this.pressed && !this.disabled) || this.flash },

    // The :focus-visible channel for the control's own styling (a Tab header's
    // focus edge): focused and the focus arrived by keyboard. Captured at the
    // focus event (the web's rule), cleared by blur — and by a pointer press on
    // this very control, the one case with no focus event (Focus.focus on the
    // already-focused target is a no-op, but the modality still cleared).

    focusVisible: boolean = false,

    // attribute — and because an attribute is the one form where authored and
    // bound are the same mechanism: `iconLeft = TrashIcon` and
    // `iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated toolbar are one slot.

    iconLeft:  string = "",
    iconRight: string = "",

    // The menu this control drops. Set it and the disclosure mark, the anchored
    // open, and the open-state styling all follow; `openMenu()` is the seam a
    // concrete control calls from its own `press()`.

    menu: View = null,

    // Derived, not written. A flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu
    // closes some other way — Escape, a pick, a click on the backdrop — and the

    // menu-dropping control wears the same mark.

    rightIcon: string = { this.iconRight != "" ? this.iconRight : this.menu != null ? "ChevronIcon" : "" },

        if (this.menu == null || this.disabled) return

    // the activation seam — concrete controls override; pointer and keyboard both land here

    press() { if (this.menu != null) this.openMenu() },

    // the control's focus silhouette — override to ring something other than

    // { x, y, w, h, rad } in the control's own coordinates.

    focusShape() { return null },

    // keyboard activation's visual acknowledgment: flash the pressed look, the
    // platform convention for buttons. Value controls whose state change is
    // the feedback (Checkbox, Switch, Radio) don't call this. `flashMs` is
    // per-control tunable. `flash` is the control's own state — the `pressed`
    // intrinsic is the pointer's truth and is read-only; a keyboard pulse is a
    // different fact, folded into `down`.

    flash:   boolean = false,
    flashMs: number  = 220,

    flashPress() {
        this.flash = true
        setTimeout(() => { this.flash = false }, this.flashMs)

    onFocus() { this.focused = true; this.focusVisible = Focus.byKeyboard() },
    onBlur()  { this.focused = false; this.focusVisible = false },

    // A click is also a focus claim — the keyboard picks up where the pointer
    // left. A menu opens here, not from `onClick`: every other control routes
    // the pointer through `press()` (`onClick() { if (!disabled) press() }`),

    // event.

    onPointerDown() {
        if (this.disabled) return
        this.focusVisible = false

        if (this.menu != null) this.openMenu()
        },

    // Down opens a menu control — the platform convention, and the reason `menu`
    // is a role rather than an icon: an author who wired a chevron by hand never

    onKeyDown(e: KeyEvent) {

        if (e.key == "Enter" || e.key == " ") this.press()

        }
    ]

# TextLabel

A `Text` that centers its ink in its parent's height — the vertical placement a
*label* wants, as opposed to a paragraph. Use it for the text inside a control
or any centered caption; use plain `Text` for flowing copy.

Why it exists. `y = center` on a plain `Text` centers the geometric box (the
ordinary meaning, matching every other view). But a label sitting in a box wants
its **letterforms** optically centered, not the font's box with its asymmetric
ascent/descent leading — otherwise the text reads a hair low. `TextLabel`
supplies a `y` that centers the cap band (cap-top to baseline), the optical
centre for a label:

    y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 }

That expression cap-centres the label: the ink sits centred by its cap band rather
than by its box, which is what reads as centred for a label. It is written out here,
once, instead of at every use site. It is a plain constraint over the Text's own live
metric facts
(`baseline`, `capHeight`, measured from the effective font), so it re-centers
when the font, the size, or the parent's height changes. Override `y` on an
instance to opt out.

The centre is the cap band because that is what the platform control themes
(Cupertino, Mountain View, Redmond) are matched against.

## y
Centres the ink on the parent's height by its cap band — baseline and cap height — rather than by the line box, which is what a label beside a control wants and a paragraph does not.
*/

class TextLabel extends Text [
    y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 }
    ]

/*
# Segmented

A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options
are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are **data**, like
`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

```declare-fragment
Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page },
    choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }),
                 ({ id: "table",    label: "Table" }),
                 ({ id: "grid",     label: "DataGrid" }) ] },
    input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
    ]
```

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

### Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a design decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view
tree, not the layout strategy whose job that is. Three reasons not to:

- **A segmented control divides evenly; a row of buttons sizes to content.** The
  two are different controls, and this one is the first.
- **The segmented convention makes it a content rule**: keep segment labels short and
  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.
- **The sliding pill.** At equal widths it translates at constant width. At
  variable widths it would have to morph its width while travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly: **a `Segmented` does not self-size to
its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

### The pill

The highlight springs a **normalized lane** — a float index — not pixels. `x` is
then `lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes `segW` and the pill **snaps** to the
right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen
segment wears a raised `surface` pill with a hairline.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one",
    Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page },
        choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }),
                     ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }),
                     ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] },
        input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }

    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ]
    ]
```

The active choice. Bind it to your own state and override `input` to own the
destination, or leave it alone and read `value` back — a `Segmented` works
standalone. Compared against each item's `choice` by identity, so any value type
works.

**Internal.** The marker a `SegmentedItem` reads to recognize its parent. A
`.declare` class cannot hold a reactive cell without declaring it, so a marker is
necessarily surface — that does not make it API.

## choices
The segments, as **records**: `{ id, label }` or `{ id, icon }` — the same vocabulary

carry a `location`, which makes that segment a real link (see `SegmentedItem.location`).

## input()
**Where the choice goes**, receiving the picked `id`. The default writes `value`;
override it to own the destination.

## pick()
Selects a choice by id, routing through `input`. The seam a segment calls.

## disabled
Disables the whole control. **A segment is not separately disable-able** — a disabled
group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops.

## opacity
Disabled dims the whole control — track, pill and every segment alike, never a

The per-segment width used when you set no `width` on the control. Because a

How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero.

One segment's width — the control's width divided by the count. What the pill and every

/*
# SegmentedItem

One choice of a `Segmented`, **materialized from that control's `choices` data — never
authored directly**, which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full

inactive choice and select it.

segments instead of popping.

Whether this segment is the group's current choice, derived from the parent by identity.

This segment's text and icon colour, brightening when it is on or hot. One slot, so a
label and an icon can never disagree.

Makes this segment a **real link**: give a choice a `location` and the segment navigates

Delivers this segment's id to the group.

Navigates if the choice carries a `location`, then presses.

Space and Enter pick; arrows rove to the adjacent segment.

Rings the segment's pill inset, not its whole box.

**Internal.** The marker a `Segmented` reads to find its own segments — not API.

As tall as the control.

Every segment the same width — the control's `segW`, its width divided by its count.

Placed by index: the control's inset plus `i` segment widths.

    // this widget reads it, so `theme.x` reads below are plain typed members.
    // Default = the house look.

    theme: Theme = { this.$provided("theme", SanFrancisco) },

    // the marker a SegmentedItem reads to recognize its parent

    isSegmented: boolean = true,

    choices: array = [],           // a bare literal: it owns a cell, so a use-site value wires
    value: object = null,
    disabled: boolean = false,

    // return to the previous place, never the previous tab. Default false: a
    // switch that is itself navigation (the docs' Guide/Reference) keeps
    // pushing.

    cornerRadius = 8,
    fill = { this.theme.control },
    opacity = { this.disabled ? (typeof this.theme.disabledOpacity == "number" ? this.theme.disabledOpacity : 0.45) : 1 },

    segMin: number = 96,           // per-segment width when the author sets none
    count:  number = { Math.max(1, ((this.choices ?? [])).length) },
    width  = { this.count * this.segMin },
    segW:   number = { (this.width - 4) / this.count },

    // Which choice is live, as an index — from the data, which is the only place
    // this question can be asked. −1 (nothing selected) parks the pill at 0 and
    // hides it rather than springing to a phantom slot.

    idx: number = { ((this.choices ?? [])).findIndex((c) => c.id === this.value) },

    // ── the delivery seam ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

    input(v: object) { this.value = v },
    pick(v: object) { this.input(v) },

    // the member walk — handlers only; a constraint may not aggregate the tree

    segs() -> array {
        const out = []
        for (const c of this.children) { if ((c).isSegment === true) out.push(c) }

    // arrows rove focus across the segments (a focused segment calls this);
    // Space/Enter on the landed segment picks — so an inactive choice is
    // reachable and selectable entirely from the keyboard

    roveFrom(seg: View, d: number) {
        const ss = this.segs()
        const i = ss.indexOf(seg)
        if (i < 0) return
        const n = Math.max(0, Math.min(ss.length - 1, i + d))

    // the current segment width, so the pill is correct at any size the moment
    // layout changes and only animates when the selection does.

    lane: number = 0,
    Spring [ attribute = lane, to = { classroot.idx < 0 ? 0 : classroot.idx },
        stiffness = 260, damping = 30, mass = 0.9, epsilon = 0.002 ],

        width = { (parent).segW },
        visible = { (parent).idx >= 0 },
        fill = { classroot.theme.surface },
        stroke = { stroke(1, classroot.theme.line) } ],

    // The index rides in the data — replication has no ordinal of its own, and
    // the pill needs one to place each segment.

    items: Dataset [ contents = { { rows: ((classroot.choices ?? [])).map((c, i) => ({ ...c, i: i })) } } ],

    // Replicated as direct children, so a segment's `parent` is the control
    // itself — the pill and the segments are siblings over one cursor.

    datapath = { this.items.value },
    SegmentedItem [ datapath = :rows[] ]

// One choice. A Control — its own tab stop, Space/Enter activating the pick, so

```declare-fragment
Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ]                             // icon only
```

nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space
reclaimed. A `menu` supplies the right icon on its own (`control.declare`).

The button's text. `""` (the default) leaves it iconless-and-wordless, which is
only useful with an `icon` — a button with neither has nothing to press.

Space between the icon and the label, when both are present.

Horizontal padding inside the button, each side. The button sizes to its content
plus twice this, so widening it is how you make a short label less cramped.

```declare-fragment
Button [ label = "OK", padH = 28 ]                  // a short word, given room
Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon", gap = 12 ]
```

The one ink decision, so a button's icon and its label always agree: the accent
text colour when `primary`, the ordinary text colour otherwise. `textColor`
follows it. Override this rather than `textColor` alone, or the icon and the

# WrappingLayout — a flow that wraps to new rows

A horizontal flow that **wraps**: children run left to right `spacing` apart,
and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row,
`rowSpacing` down. With room for
one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow
on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is
2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `justify`
sets each finished row along the flow — `start`, `center`, `end`, or `fill`,
which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does;
`indent` and `hangingIndent` inset the first row and every row after it, the
two shapes a paragraph takes.

that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and a flow answers to it on
both axes: rows **wrap at the content width** — the room between the left and
right insets, never the view's own width — and a view that sizes itself from
the flow grows by the vertical pair, so no row runs under the inset.

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, rowSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]

```

## spacing
The horizontal gap between children in a row.

## rowSpacing
The vertical gap between rows. The two gaps are independent: a uniform grid writes
the same number for both, and a negative `rowSpacing` pulls rows into each other,
which is what a large display face wants when it wraps — the row height a big face
reports is looser than the line wants to sit.

## justify
How a finished row sits along the flow: `start` (the default, left), `center`, `end`
(right), or `fill` — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its
children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

## indent
The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The
first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see `hangingIndent`).

## hangingIndent
The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography
entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two
compose: `indent` sets where the first row starts, `hangingIndent` where the rest do.

`center`, `end`, or `baseline`, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a

refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the
baseline-shifted children. When the flow **never wrapped** — one row, which is the whole
content — `center` and `end` align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row
in a `height = 90` bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height
from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal.

## place()
Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. **It owns
both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than
looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and
has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row.

    rowSpacing: number = 0,
    justify: Justify = start,

                else if (al == "end") off = lineH - heights[j]

            // the child's footprint (scale/rotation composed, position-free —
            // place() must not read the x/y it writes), and the transform's own
            // lead offset, compensated so the visible box lands on the flow
            const f = (c).footprint()
            const cw = f.width
            const ch = f.height
            const leadX = f.x
            const leadY = f.y
            // wrap when this child (with its leading gap) would overflow — never
            // on a row's first child, so one over-wide child just overflows
            if (!firstInRow && cx + sp + cw > w) { const lh = finish(i, cx, false); cx = indN; cy = cy + lh + ls; rowH = 0; rowBase = 0; firstInRow = true; rowStart = i }

            rowH = Math.max(rowH, ch)

## Backdrop and section heads

The blueprint grid draws itself; a `SectionHead` is the tight

/*
The blueprint backdrop is VIEWPORT-sized and pinned, never document-sized.

`draw()` rasterises into a canvas the size of the view's bounds at device pixel
ratio, so a backdrop stretched over a whole document would allocate a backing
store for the whole document: the language view is 16,711px tall, which at 2x
is a 2882 x 33,422 canvas — 96 megapixels, ~385 MB, reallocated every time the
view is shown or hidden, and about a second of blocked main thread each way.
It would also exceed Chrome's 32,767px maximum canvas dimension. Viewport-sized
and pinned, the same two moments measure 57 ms and 21 ms.

A uniform 32px lattice looks the same pinned as it does scrolling, so this
costs nothing visually — it is the same paper, drawn once.

Every view on the site that wears the paper wears the SAME paper, so the
geometry is the class's and a use site says only one thing: `bottom`, the
content's own extent it must not run past. It follows the scroll rather than
spanning the document — `ignoreScroll` would lift it out of paint order and
composite it OVER the content; as an ordinary child it stays behind. Snapped to
the 32px lattice so the paper is pixel-identical to the document-tall version —
the same lines in the same places — while only one viewport is ever rasterised.

The clamp is the part that has to be right. Unclamped, the backdrop's bottom is
`scrollY` + a viewport, which feeds the scroller's auto-extent — so every trip
to the bottom grew the page another 32px and left dead space under the footer
(measured: 5243 → 5412 over six trips). Reading the content's extent is what the
document-tall version did too, and it is not a cycle: the content never reads
the backdrop.
*/

class GridBg extends View [

    // the bottom of the content this paper backs, in the same space as this
    // view's own y — the one number a use site supplies

    bottom: number = 0,

    width = 100%,
    height = { this.root.height + 32 },
    y = { Math.max(0, Math.min(Math.floor(this.root.scrollY / 32) * 32, this.bottom - this.height)) },

    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.fillStyle = this.$provided("theme").grid
        for (let gx = 0; gx <= this.width;  gx += 32) d.fillRect(gx, 0, 1, this.height)
        for (let gy = 0; gy <= this.height; gy += 32) d.fillRect(0, gy, this.width, 1)
        }
    ]

## The page

The palette lives once as a provided `theme` token record — every semantic

// THE HEADLINE LIVES HERE, ONCE. The hero reads it, and `appName` carries it
// into `document.title` at boot (runtime/src/boot.ts — "the ONE place that
// mapping lives"), which is also what the crawl extraction reports as the
// page's title and what the bake stamps into index.html's <title> and social
// cards. Stating it anywhere else would be a copy that only crawlers and LLMs
// ever read — the runtime overwrites document.title at boot, so a visitor
// would never see it drift. Exactly the readers this page is for.

App [ tagline: string = "a UI language for you and your AI",
    edges = cover,
    revealInset = 80,
    appName = { "Declare — " + this.root.tagline },

    // site's own presentation is dark — the shots, the video, the blueprint
    // grid and the plate shadows are all composed for it — so a light system
    // no longer decides how a first-time reader sees it. The header's switch
    // still flips to light and from then on the choice holds. Every colour
    // below reads the theme, so the whole page (and the hosted Architecture
    // article, through its island) follows.

    // the page's tokens win, and the widgets the page borrows find the rest

    theme = { this.root.isDark ? ({ ...SanFranciscoDark, ...Ink }) : ({ ...SanFrancisco, ...Paper }) },
    fill = { this.$provided("theme").ink },

    // quick-start guide, rendered the same way) — the app’s slice of the

    // clean URL at "home" and `#why`/`#language` elsewhere, seeds it from a deep
